profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a hospital preparing to extend the COAST bedside shift report process from a successful medical-surgical pilot to a 24-bed cardiac step-down unit. The context is a four-week pre-launch window in which operations and quality teams need to align staff education, bedside materials, EHR support, and audit reporting after bedside report had been inconsistently practiced since the pandemic. The agenda is to confirm what the unit will use as the COAST tool, how compliance will be tracked, which staff are included in the initial night-shift rollout, and how weekly audits will be completed and shared. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for launch timing, training coverage, audit cadence, and dashboard reporting, even though several second-order assumptions remain misaligned.

members.name: Alyssa Romero
members.expertise: Inpatient nursing operations, shift handoff workflow, staff coaching, bedside safety practices
members.background: Alyssa is an RN with 12 years in acute care and the last 3 years managing a cardiac step-down unit; she helped restore bedside practices after pandemic restrictions eased and is focused on reducing falls, missed oxygen issues, and overtime at shift change.
members.private_state: She wants the rollout to feel practical and behavior-based so staff actually do bedside report consistently, and she is worried that if the process becomes too documentation-heavy or excludes temporary staff, the unit will look compliant on paper without changing handoff quality.
hidden_assumptions: When people say COAST compliance, they mean a live bedside handoff in which all five COAST elements are verbally covered with the patient present.
The updated COAST tool is the laminated bedside cue card and report script that nurses physically use during handoff, not the EHR smartphrase.
If the rollout is for all night-shift RNs, that naturally includes travelers and float-pool nurses because they give and receive report like everyone else.
A weekly audit means someone observes an actual bedside report so missed elements can be corrected in real time.

members.name: Daniel Cho
members.role: Clinical Informatics RN and Quality Improvement Coordinator
members.expertise: Nursing documentation workflows, audit design, EHR build, compliance dashboards, sustainment reporting
members.background: Daniel is an RN who moved into informatics and quality six years ago; he supported the original COAST pilot by building handoff note fields and producing monthly compliance summaries for nursing leadership.
members.private_state: He wants a low-burden rollout that can be monitored reliably through existing data systems, and he is concerned that live observation and ad hoc materials will create inconsistent measurement and make sustainment reports difficult to defend.
hidden_assumptions: When people say COAST compliance, they mean completion of the COAST handoff elements in the documented handoff workflow closely enough to populate the dashboard.
The updated COAST tool is the revised EHR handoff note smartphrase and flowsheet prompts deployed last month.
If the rollout is for all night-shift RNs, that means the permanent unit staff roster assigned through the learning system; travelers and float staff are a separate onboarding stream.
A weekly audit can appropriately be done through chart review and EHR completion data, with only occasional spot observation if needed.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss improving and reporting COAST compliance.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means bedside behavioral fidelity: all five COAST elements are verbally covered during an in-room shift report with the patient.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means measurable workflow completion: the COAST elements are documented in the handoff note well enough to count on the dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Compliance is a familiar quality-improvement term, so each assumes the other is using the hospital's usual meaning; because both behavior and documentation often move together, the surface agreement feels sufficient.

misalignment_points.topic: Which COAST tool is being finalized
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using or distributing the updated COAST tool.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking about the laminated bedside cue card and paper badge-backer script that charge nurses will hand out.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking about the updated EHR COAST smartphrase and handoff template revision already loaded in the test-to-live release.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are legitimately called the COAST tool on different teams, and in rollout conversations people often blur educational materials and documentation tools together.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included in the night-shift rollout
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to launch with all night-shift RNs first.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes permanent staff, travelers, and float-pool nurses who regularly cover the unit at night.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes only nurses on the unit's permanent night-shift roster because that is who can be auto-assigned training and tracked cleanly in reports.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In staffing conversations, 'all night-shift RNs' sounds complete and ordinary, and neither expects the other to be drawing a different administrative boundary around the same group.

misalignment_points.topic: How the weekly audit will be carried out
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to do a weekly COAST audit for the first month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects direct observation of live bedside shift reports by charge nurses or educators using a checklist.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a weekly chart-based audit drawn from EHR handoff documentation, with observation reserved for rare validation checks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Audit is a shared quality term that names the goal rather than the method, and both methods are common enough in hospital projects that each hears the other's statement as confirming their own standard approach.

turns.inner_thought: Our step-down nurses are ready for a reset on real bedside report now that routines have stabilized. I need this to land as a practical behavior on nights in early May, not another thing that looks good in paperwork and doesn't change what happens in the room. If we keep it focused on the bedside COAST script and coach to it consistently, we can cut missed oxygen checks and sloppy handoff drift without blowing up shift change.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. Cardiac step-down is in a good spot to get bedside report back to a more consistent place, and I'd like to line up the COAST launch plan for nights in early May.

turns.inner_thought: If we're doing this in four weeks, I need clarity on whether we're pointing people to the revised COAST smartphrase and flowsheet prompts, how the weekly audit will run, and exactly what data will count toward compliance on the dashboard. I want this to be measurable through the existing EHR workflow so leadership gets defensible trends without building a manual observation machine.
turns.utterance: That timing should be workable from the quality side. If we can confirm the updated COAST tool, the weekly audit process, and what will feed the compliance dashboard, I can get the reporting pieces lined up.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I'll have charge nurses distribute the laminated bedside cue cards and badge backers at huddle and reinforce using them in the patient room. That's the updated COAST tool in my mind—the thing staff can actually hold during report so they cover code status, oxygen, access, safety, and tubes/drains in a tight, repeatable way.
turns.utterance: Perfect. My plan is to have the charge nurses hand out the updated COAST tool in huddle and then use it at the bedside so the report stays tight and consistent.

turns.inner_thought: Great, she's aligned with using the updated EHR COAST tool. Once the revised handoff smartphrase is live for the unit, the dashboard should pick up element completion cleanly from the handoff workflow. That gives us a straightforward week-over-week compliance trend without asking managers to maintain separate paper tracking.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Once the updated COAST tool is live for the unit, improving and reporting COAST compliance should be pretty easy to trend week over week from the handoff workflow.

turns.inner_thought: I want nights first because that's where we can build the bedside habit reliably. On this unit, that includes whoever is regularly giving and receiving report overnight—core staff, travelers, and float nurses. Patients don't experience separate categories, and if we leave temporary staff out, the whole thing will look uneven immediately.
turns.utterance: I’d like to launch with all night-shift RNs first. They have the most predictable timing for report, and if we get that group steady, they can model it for days.

turns.inner_thought: Starting with the permanent night roster is ideal. I can assign the learning packet through the learning system to all night-shift RNs on that unit and carve their data out on the dashboard before we broaden to days. Keeping the initial group tied to the roster will make the reporting cleaner and avoid noise from people who belong to separate onboarding streams.
turns.utterance: I’m good with that. I can assign the learning packet to all night-shift RNs and split out their COAST compliance on the dashboard before we expand to day shift.

turns.inner_thought: For the first month, I need charge nurses or the educator watching actual bedside reports once a week. That's the only way to know whether staff are really covering all five COAST elements in the room with the patient there, and it lets us coach misses immediately instead of waiting for bad habits to set. A chart won't tell me if oxygen or safety was actually discussed at the bedside.
turns.utterance: And for that first month, I want a weekly COAST audit so the charge nurses can catch whether code status, oxygen, access, safety, and tubes or drains are actually being covered.

turns.inner_thought: Weekly chart-based review will work well. I can pull Monday-through-Sunday handoff documentation every Tuesday, summarize compliance by element, and send it back quickly enough for the unit to react. If something looks off, we can always validate with a spot check, but the core audit should stay in the data so it remains consistent and sustainable.
turns.utterance: A weekly COAST audit works. I can pull Monday-through-Sunday results each Tuesday so we can look at COAST compliance and any misses by element.

turns.inner_thought: I also need travelers getting the same laminated bedside cue during orientation, otherwise nights won't feel consistent from the patient side and permanent staff will start improvising around whoever they're paired with. When I say all night-shift RNs, I mean everyone handing off on nights, not just the home unit roster.
turns.utterance: One other piece—I also want travelers to get the same updated COAST tool in orientation so the night rollout feels uniform from the patient perspective.

turns.inner_thought: Let's see the first week's dashboard numbers from the permanent night staff before changing too much. If compliance rates or element completion look uneven, we can tighten the learning packet or tip sheet. Travelers can be handled through their usual onboarding path later if needed; I don't want to muddy the initial data set while we're trying to judge whether the rollout is working.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. Once the first week’s numbers come through, we’ll be able to see how the rollout is landing and decide whether the education needs any tweaks.
